utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. It is Wednesday, 16th of January, 2008. I'd like to greet the Prosecution, Defence counsel, as well as all the accused present today. I would also like to greet everybody else in and around the courtroom. I believe Ms. Alaburic still has eight minutes. Let's have the witness brought in, please. The Chamber had a problem with the time left for Pusic and Coric. I believe that we understood that Mr. Pusic had ceded all his time, but we didn't know about the other accused. So I'm turning towards the Defence counsel. What can be said about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]: Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Coric cedes its time to the Petkovic defence and to the Praljak defence as well, all its time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If I might explain in order to avoid any misunderstanding. We ceded our time to the Defence of Mr. Petkovic, all our time. We didn't deal with the Coric Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Mr. Coric had 40 minutes. This time is ceded to the other Defence counsel. However, we have Mrs. Alaburic left only if I understood correctly. Mrs. Alaburic, how much time are you going to need?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to you. I think that I will complete my cross-examination within the next 10 minutes or so, and I have cut short my cross-examination due to the circumstances so that the rest of the time can be used by the Praljak Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Thornberry. Unfortunately, we just have a little more time to carry on our discussion. We looked at the transcript yesterday from the meeting of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Presidency and I'm going to summarise the part that I wanted to read out. "In continuation, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, when taking the floor, summarised and said that the army of Republika Srpska was too strong both with respect to the number of men it had and with regard to the technical equipment it had at its disposal and that the BH army, that it could rout the army, and that is why the Muslim side was forced to accept some sort of peaceful solution which otherwise it would not be willing to do, a peaceful solution which would not lead to a united unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina which was the political goal of Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslim side in the conflict." Now, my question to you is this: Did you know -- were you aware that the Muslim side in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina considered the Serb army too strong to stand up to, but that it also considered that it was superior in relation to the HVO and that if it entered into a conflict with the HVO it could achieve its territorial goals in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what are -- what is the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The question was probably too long. Let me repeat it again. My question is this: Were you aware that the Muslim side in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina considered the Serbs to be too strong to stand up to, but that on the other hand, it thought that it could realise its territorial ambitions, or some of them, in confronting the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would answer in the affirmative to both questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could I just ask counsel for a reference to the page number of the transcript that -- that was just being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are contained on page 20 of the transcript, where an extensive explanation is given about the Serb army, how many thousand soldiers, how many artillery pieces, how many tanks and so on. And in other parts of the transcript, particularly at the beginning, we can see the relationship towards the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Thornberry, let us now take a look at another document. It's an UNPROFOR document which will help us clarify what it was exactly that the BH army wanted, at least when it came to territory. Now, look at my set of documents, please, and the number of the document I'd like you to look at is P 5033.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5033. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Tell me, please, Mr. Thornberry, do you recognise the document? And from the heading we can see that it is a document sent to you, and it was sent by Mr. Ed Joseph. Do you remember the document perhaps?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've lost the document itself. I thought I had it in my hand, but -- yes, if I could have the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's first of all see whether you remember the document since it was addressed to you as it says in the document itself on the title page.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would take me 40 minutes to read through the whole of this document from Ed Joseph. I'm sorry. Would you like me to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no, Witness, that won't be necessary. All I wanted was for you to confirm that the document was indeed sent to you. Now, the document is a note about meetings, as it says in the introductory part, with the military commanders in Mostar, meetings with Mostar military commanders, Miljenko Lasic from the HVO, and Mr. Pasalic from the BH army. Now, I'm interested in Mr. Pasalic. So would you please take a look at paragraph 11 of this document now, please. Paragraph 11 of the document says what Pasalic stated, who said access to the sea under Bosnian control is considered vital. Pasalic does not pay too much attention to the guaranteed corridors by the international community even if there were American troops on the ground. Now, tell us, Mr. Thornberry, please, did you have other information to the effect that the BH army considered the break through of the corridor to the Adriatic Sea, which would be under its control as its priority in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what its priority might be. That was for them to determine. Broadly speaking, however, in paragraph 11 this seems -- I'm not sure that I would use the same language perhaps, but I think that it is an accurate statement, broadly speaking, of the longer-term strategy of those involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In what we've just read out, mention is made of American troops on the ground. Now, based on your knowledge, the arrival of American troops in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was that indeed an option for resolving the crisis in BH?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I heard. There were, of course, as you certainly knew -- there is now a detachment of United States troops, but that is elsewhere within the region, but it came as a result of overall planning on the part of several leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now take a look at the last point in this document, or paragraph. It's number 17 where it says after mentioning that the Serbs have a vested interest in the outcome in southern Bosnia-Herzegovina, Pasalic admitted that the Chetniks could help the Armija. Tell us, please, Witness, did you know -- or, rather, let's start off by asking you, do you know who the Chetniks are as it -- as they are mentioned in this paragraph, paragraph 17?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an idea, yes. But unfortunately, I don't know whether it's me or whether it's the documents -- I can't find a -- with a paragraph of that -- with that number. I have 16. Is it -- is it a paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I was reading from the Croatian text, and the numbers are different. I've just taken a look at the English text and that's true. It is paragraph 16. Now, you say you do have some idea of who the Chetniks were. Tell me, did Mr. Pasalic mean the Serbs when he said "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You'd have to ask him had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the term or concept "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a few times.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you understood this term?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the term to refer to probably Serb irregular troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's assume that Mr. Pasalic, when he said"Chetniks," meant to say the Armija of Republika Srpska or, rather, the Serbs. Now, I'd like you to help us out and help us establish the following: Did you know that the army of Republika Srpska, or Pasalic -- as Pasalic calls them, the Chetniks, helped the BH army in certain combat operations in Herzegovina in -- in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard that story. I didn't know whether it was true or not but again I suggest you ask them. I wouldn't want to commit myself on this subject without hearing what their intent was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, even if we wanted to hear Mr. Pasalic, we couldn't. Mr. Thornberry, thank you for your answers, and I'd like to inform the Trial Chamber that that completes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak's Defence counsel will have 40 minutes plus 40 minutes ceded as it seems by Coric's Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will start the cross-examination off, and in a while I'll table a request to allow General Praljak to carry on the cross-examination and why you should allow him to do so in line with or contrary to your ruling of May last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Thornberry, during your testimony here over the past two days, several times you made some assessments which I'd like to summarise by stating some of the characteristic words. I think you said that the situation was one of confusion several times, that the situation was bizarre. That was on page 18 of yesterday's transcript, for example, that not everything was as it seemed. For the record that's on page 24 of yesterday's transcript. And similar assessments. I think that you describe that in very clear terms. Now, with respect to the confusion that existed, I would like to ask you a question. Was that only your opinion? Did you -- was it only you that felt this confusion and that nothing was as it seemed at first glance, or do you believe, or perhaps do you know that other foreign observers, monitors, and I'm thinking of your colleagues from UNPROFOR first and foremost, as well as those from the ECMM, that those people from that circle of the international community shared your opinion? Did they? Were others conscious of the fact that this was a state of confusion and that it was difficult to make any clear-cut conclusions? Could you explain that a little to us, please?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me try. I think that my colleagues in UNPROFOR probably thought along similar lines to those indicated here. I certainly wouldn't imagine that they agreed absolutely with them either when they were made or later, because on the whole, United Nations personnel are rather single-minded. So I don't -- I'm not sure that there would be that degree of consensus. Not to begin with in any event. Later, when we'd had a chance to talk things out, then there might have been a little bit more clarity. I'm not sure. Was there, sir, another question within that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you. I think that you answered my question in very precise terms. I'd like now to touch upon your statement for a moment, the one you gave to the Prosecutor. It is P 10041, and it will be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like to explain in view of the limitations you set on us. I'd like to explain that the -- that the Prosecution, as far as I understand their letter, wishes to admit this under the subtitle of "the warring factions' intentions towards Bosnia," beginning on page 11. However, as far as I understand their letter, their previous letter, it is not their intention to tender into evidence the introductory paragraph which begins on page 10 and goes on to page 11. And looking at the text, I think that that is an integral part of the text, because first of all we have "the UN mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina," a broader heading, and then going down to specifics "The warring factions' intentions towards Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 11 of your statement, Mr. Thornberry -- have you got that to hand? I'd like to draw your attention to paragraphs 39 and 40. First of all, in paragraph 39, as far as I understand your statement, you in fact state expressly that you did not pay any special attention to the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina until the beginning of 1993, and from the rest of your statement we come to understand that that is because you were more focused on UNPA zones in Croatia. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I used the phrase "significant attention." It might be slightly overstated because I'm referring here to Bosnia and Herzegovina and that there had been significant -- not significant attention to them. It's not -- I wouldn't -- I wouldn't use this phrase, actually, if I were beginning again. It's too strong, it's too blunt, and I would rather see it having been expressed in a more nuanced way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would the following formulation correspond to that, and that's how -- how I understand it: Until early 1993, the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, within the frameworks of the job you had to do there, were not in the focus of your attention. They weren't primary to you, if I can put it that way. Would you agree with that definition of mine? On the basis of what you've just told me.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very nearly, sir, very nearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. From this statement further on, and from what you've been telling us over the past two days here, you travelled for the first time to Bosnia personally in August 1993, as you've told us; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I've told you that, then I'm sorry, it's not correct, because the leadership of the UNPROFOR, first of all, went to -- to Bosnia, and also I remember, I think -- well, we certainly went to Bosnia, and -- and for a while there was a lot of movement to and fro across the lines to a -- to a substantial degree, because you -- we were, you see, setting up a mission, and it -- it requires different kind of work than if one is taking over a mission and running it then. This -- this formulation, again I -- I find it a little bit too blunt, and because of that bluntness it loses some of its meaning, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I wasn't precise enough. From these exhibits, the ones we've seen so far without a doubt UNPROFOR as an institution was present, but I would like -- I wanted to ask about you personally. Did you personally go before August?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went there about the 14th or 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you were there in March. I seem to think that you were there in June as well. And then in August.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very likely that I was there in June and certain that I was there in August, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, in the next paragraph, I'd like to draw attention to your is second sentence -- or, rather, the last sentence in that paragraph where you say that it was your impression that "we," and I think you mean UNPROFOR, "did not understand very much of the situation..." and you go on to say, "... My experience told me not to believe what was being reported fully, rather, I needed to see things for myself." Now, would that be correct? Have I interpreted what you say in your report correctly?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think that probably is fairly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, maybe just a couple of points for clarification purposes. On the first day of your examination, at page 32 of the transcript, at one point when you describe the circumstances of the visit to the hospital, I believe, you said that the children had been frequent targets of unidentified snipers. Could you please explain this? Was this your personal assessment? What was this based on? Was it based on the information that you received from the people you talked to, or perhaps did you yourself witness any such incidents in which children were deliberately targeted by anyone, any side?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to say deliberately. There would have to be a big gap for -- to fill in there, but the information that I had was not based upon what I saw or heard or whatever, but, rather, upon what very senior people, very experienced people, who had been in the area for some time, what they told me when I sought briefings from them, because UNPROFOR, as you know, was a very big organisation even in its first six months, and it was doing a great deal of information gathering, and I think I was seeking to make the best value out of the information that my -- my colleagues had. I was senior political advisor, and the obligation was upon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can I conclude then that you received this information indirectly? This was second-hand information that you received from your people on the ground, to simplify matters. And just one more question to get a really clear picture. Do you perhaps remember any piece of information, any report that you received from your people on the ground where they spoke about a specific incident, today at 12.00 at such-and-such location, or did those reports also contain merely assessments or opinions to the fact that children someplace -- I mean, it is well -- a well-known fact that children were casualties of war, but that they were actually targeted?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to surgeons at the hospital in Mostar, there was a very cruel practice of targeting young people, children, but not only, not only. It was a much more widespread problem. And as you say, it was largely based on hearsay that I arrived at those conclusions, but I was confident in my mind that they were true given the sources that they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine. To clarify things, then, since you visited two hospitals in Mostar, first the one in West Mostar, and I think that we also saw some children on the footage there, and then you went on to visit the hospital in East Mostar, did you hear that on both sides or in just one of those hospitals? Well, it's a very simple answer. I know, I don't know, I can't remember. I know that it's difficult to perhaps recall some things. If you can't recall it, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: After X number of years I'm afraid I have to concede that I don't remember whether I was told this on one side or the other side of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I don't want to go into any more details because of the limited topic that we're exploring, but I would like to move that my client, the accused Mr. Praljak, be allowed to ask some questions bearing in mind your decision of the 10th of May last year. Let me remind you that Mr. Praljak was in the field at that time. We saw a video clip proving that Mr. Praljak was there. He was a participant of some of the events that this witness was talking about, quite specifically the passage of the humanitarian convoy. Questions will be based on the documents that the OTP planned to tender through this witness, so they -- the questions are linked to the topics. And this will be within the framework of the decision of the Chamber restricting the cross-examination by the accused in this -- in this trial. And I believe that Mr. Praljak is definitely qualified. He has specific expert knowledge of the events and of the topics that we're discussing here. So both of the conditions have been met to allow him to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has deliberated and holds that Mr. Praljak may put questions to the witness on issues relating to the convoys, because we have seen videos where he intervened personally. So General Praljak can address the issue of the convoys and meetings with the witness in the event that he did meet the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Of course I will not be using up all of the time because there are not so many questions that remain to be asked. Some technical matters are left to be examined regarding the convoy and the documents about the convoy. I will not be going any further from that topic. I will start with the convoy, but I will move on from that too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, there is a document with the number -- a document about a meeting in Makarska. It was a big meeting. This is document P 04027. There's no need for you to go looking for this document. It's there just for the record. It's P 04027. It's the meeting in Makarska where an agreement was reached. Let me just check the date. The date is the 8th of August, 1993. Were you aware of that meeting, and were you aware of the fact that that unimpeded passage of convoys through all the areas under HVO control at that time was agreed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- sir, I don't think I remember that particular meeting. I don't want to be categorical because a number of things do come back into my memory as we proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. It doesn't the matter. According to document P 04027 a meeting was held on the 8th of August in Makarska, and an agreement was reached to let the convoys through. You arrived in Mostar later than that. So my question to you is the following: Were you aware or are you aware that after that meeting the convoys that were set up either in Split or in Ploce or in Metkovic headed both towards Mostar and Central Bosnia, but they had to go back because on the 13th of August the BH army launched a strong offensive at Buna-Blagaj area to the south of Mostar? So there was this big problem of the convoys always having to wait for such a long time, but did your people who reported to you actually tell you that the convoys that had headed out on the 11th, the 12th, had to turn back because the BH army on the 13th of August cut off the road at Blagaj, that's the famous Mostar -- the road leading to the sea from Mostar, and that there was fierce fighting in that area in that time because the BH army was trying to break through towards Stolac and Capljina? I don't know. If you know that, please say so. If you don't know that, I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to say I don't remember knowing that. I don't know it about it -- I don't know about it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Regarding the convoys, could we now look at document P 03858. Those are the press releases. We have three such press releases. One is dated on the 21st of August, one the 20th of August, and the third one is dated the 19th of August. These are all UNPROFOR press releases. In those documents, as we will see in the 21st of August, 1993, release, in the first passage it says the area that has for almost three months been a no-go area for the United Nations and other humanitarian agencies. So where we hear that for three months this area had been a no-go area for any convoys. No convoys could go in. Do you know that the first paragraph of this UNPROFOR press release dated the 21st of August -- are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, will you forgive me just a moment, please, while we locate those documents. I have -- I have document 0079696.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: P 038 -- yeah, that's the one. It says in the first paragraph the area, that's Mostar, "...an area that has been closed to the United Nations and humanitarian agencies for almost three months." And in the document under the same number, that is dated the 19th of August, in the second paragraph we have the sentence: "This convoy of seven vehicles is the first UNPROFOR convoy to get into the town over the past -- in the past two months." So from the same source we hear that this -- this same area was not closed to UNPROFOR convoys for three months but for two months. But at any rate, my question to you is the following: Were you told there that the convoys -- Mr. Thornberry, please. My question is as follows: Did those people who asked themselves how long the convoys were unable to go there, did they tell you that until the 30th of June, 1993, and we heard about that a lot here in courtroom, this was when the BH army attacked Bijelo Polje and so on, that up until that time convoys passed through Mostar on route to Central Bosnia and that they were able to enter East Mostar? Did anyone tell you that tell you that up until the 30th of June, up until the attack of the BH army on the HVO, that the convoys were able to pass through Mostar and actually enter into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not told that, speaking for myself. I don't think any of my colleagues were informed of that. No, I can't -- I'm afraid I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. It is my assumption that if it is indeed so that up until the 30th of June, the convoys were able to pass through and enter into Mostar, and then after the 13th [as interpreted] they were unable to do so because of the fighting, that this would mean that the convoy that entered -- entered into Mostar on the 20th and the 21st actually was the first convoy after a month and some 20 days. But if you don't know about that, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a question with regard to the transcript. On page 17, line 9, you speak of the 30th of June, and then line 10, after the 13th. Was that what you said, or were you both times referring to the 30th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm having some difficulty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Its --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- A question to Mr. Praljak actually.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour my question was whether Mr. Thornberry was aware that up until the 30th of August the convoys passed through and entered Mostar, and then on the 11th of August, August, after the meeting in Makarska, they headed out again and then they were turned back because of the fighting. So the break lasted about a month and ten days. And then after a month and 20 days the first convoy went in. So I was trying to clarify whether it was three months, as we can read in the first press release, two months as we can read in the second press release, or whether it was one month and 20 days. So I'm just trying to ascertain whether it is actually true that the convoys were unable to get into East Mostar for one month and 20 days, and for the most part this was due to the fighting to BH army attacks, but Mr. Thornberry was unable to assist me, and that -- we will have to explore that through other witnesses. So this is what I wanted to check, the length of time that convoys were unable to get in. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, just one more detail that remained unclarified from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the UNPROFOR press release of the 21st of August where you were quoted, your name is on here, and it is stated today, on the 21st of August, you visited East Mostar, and this seems to indicate that so far the humanitarian aid agencies and the United Nations had not been able to enter the city for three months. As Mr. Praljak has told us that there was an ABiH attack on the 13th of August at Buna Blagaj what I would like to know is this. Whether this press release, which is an UNPROFOR press release, seems to indicate that the fact that the humanitarian aid convoys were unable to enter Mostar, that this is due to the ABiH by because of its operation on the ground prevented the convoy from entering the city. What do you have to say to that, because the way it is phrased in paragraph one does not actually state what the reason behind this is, why the agencies and the UN were unable to enter Mostar for a period of three months. Is it due to the HVO, to the ABiH, X, Y, Z? I don't know. What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for that question. First of all, I hadn't noticed that there was an inconsistency of that kind, and there shouldn't have been, but it was written probably on someone's knee in an APC or something like that. So the circumstances were probably not very favourable. What is, however, important, I think, is that the -- is that it is known that the Spanish detachment, the one which went in first and went in with seven APCs, that the Spanish had had a series of very unfortunate events, and in the previous six weeks or two months, as a result of which they themselves had prevented -- they had stopped themselves going through into -- into Mostar centrally. That wasn't the only reason why they had stopped. I was there myself for several days, and it didn't -- it rarely seemed as if it were a normal entry, and there were -- there were shelling, in fact, of the town while UNPROFOR's convoy was present on the ground. So, yes, you are quite right, there is this mistake, but no, I don't think that that was the -- a determining factor in the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer doesn't shed much light on my question. What I would like to know is this: Who was preventing the UN agencies from entering Mostar, or who was preventing UNPROFOR from entering Mostar, and you respond by saying that only the Spanish Battalion was able to enter, but you did not tell me why the Spanish Battalion did not enter the town. You cannot tell me why. What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the reason is -- is to me fairly clear. The circumstances of a bombardment in Mostar were pretty compelling, and armoured personnel carriers, even armoured personnel carriers avoided such conflicts. So although I understand and appreciate and agree with part of Mr. President's statement -- question, I think the issue was wider than that and the implications a bit wider also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, just one more question in this regard. When you got there did the UNPROFOR officers or the people who were there tell you that throughout that time, from the fall of Bugojno and onwards, there was a very strong offensive by the BH army going on from the Central Bosnia area to Mostar? And the Judges have already heard about that. So that this whole story after the 30th of June was in fact marked by fierce fighting on a front line that extended from Uscoplje, Bugojno, all the way south to Mostar, 200 kilometres or so of the front line, where the BH army was trying to gain advantage to push back the HVO and to set up the corridor leading to the sea. So were you informed about combat activities, the fighting in any way?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we were, sir. I think that when we had our first meeting at your headquarters, your colleagues were there, a number of your colleagues were there, and they wanted us to understand that the reason for their reluctance to have us enter the city was your concern, which I think I shared, for injury, damage, death, et cetera. It was a very bad situation. And I think that was the main reason, was not what we were told by the doctors, but we were told by the doctors a great deal about the damage done to -- to persons in the city, and also including children, that those observations, as I've already said, did not in main come from direct observation. They came from a collection of information, a collection of information, which our knowledge and experience and that of our Spaniards -- Spanish colleagues, those things were part of -- of an assessment that one makes. How does one know anything? Basically this is now we get -- try to get to know when we put a vehicle into -- into harm's way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me now ask you the following: The Spanish Battalion inform you that on the 30th of June, after that attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the witness has just something which is rather important, and I'd like to ask him a question in greater detail. The consequences of this can be very great. You said that at the headquarters of -- you had talked to the HVO officers that were there. I don't know whether Mr. Praljak was there or not, and that he would have indicated to you that the situation was very bad, and he would have, so to speak, told you that it was difficult to enter Mostar because people could get injured or could be killed. Can you confirm today that the HVO told you that it was extremely difficult for you and all the other people to enter East Mostar because of the situation which had to do with the offensive launched by the ABiH? Can you confirm this? This is what I understood, but I stand to be corrected. This does have consequences, so can you either confirm or deny this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The language used by the colleague, Mr. Praljak, the language used by him and by his colleagues at our first meeting at the headquarters of the HV [sic] at that -- in -- on the west side of Mostar, the language used was a different one. Very significant also, sir. That is to say, we were told, but whether it was by Mr. Praljak or others of his colleagues, I don't know, we were told that they could not guarantee our safety. That is a shorthand for something quite significant, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they told you that they could not guarantee your safety. Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why not? Sir, there was a battle around, going on around us. Not -- when I say around, I don't necessarily mean around in the sense of the size of this courtroom, but in that part of East Mostar and indeed that part of West Mostar in which fighting was taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And when the HVO officers told you that, were there representatives of the Spanish Battalion together with you, or were you the only person to have heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't the only person. The -- the battalion leader, Angelo -- I've forgotten his name for a moment, Morales, he would come with us everywhere. I mean, he was the co-leader of this movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there is a Spanish commander with you when the HVO told you there is some fighting around. The British Battalion didn't say otherwise. They agreed with what was said at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The British Battalion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction, Spanish Battalion. Correction, Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes they did tell us. They warned us that we were putting ourselves at considerable risk. The Spanish colonel was very much aware of it, because the Spaniards had been -- had actually lost some men in the previous six weeks or so, and they were having to write the letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for intervening, but I'd just like us to note that there was a mistake in the record on page 22, line 13. It said the HV, whereas the witness was talking about the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very indeed. Yes, I had realised that. Yes, of course it should have been HVO instead of HV. When you said that there was the headquarters, it was the HVO headquarters, right, and the no the HV headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask two more questions. There's a document that's not in the binder, so would you look for it, please, 4D 00736. May we have that document put up on e-court. 4D 00736. And I'm going to ask you something about that document but let me start off with this: When those convoys were being prepared, Mr. Thornberry, were you clearly informed that the HVO unilaterally would take a decision about a truce, a cease-fire, and cease all combat activities while you were there on your missions? That's the first question. And number two, was that the reason General Petkovic asked for a member of the SpaBat, an officer from the Spanish Battalion, be present throughout? That is the whole time at the headquarters of Mostar HVO? So did we tell you clearly that we would cease all military activities unilaterally regardless of any damages that this might cause? Is that true? While you were there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say, sir, that I cannot remember that part of the incursion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't remember, you don't. We'll come back to that. Now, the document is P 09495. P 09495. That's the document I'd like to look at next. The date is the 20th of August, 1993. It is in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could somebody help the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is sent Thornberry, Medjugorje, and it says in paragraph 3: "The HVO warned that while they would guarantee our security up to the CFL, they could not guarantee on the other side. They said they would not return fire while we were there, they would not return fire while we were there, but would react if the Presidency forces, the BH army forces, sought to take advantage of our presence by forward movement or marching forward. During this event an officer, a liaison officer from SpaBat will be present at the HVO HQ." P 094 -- 09495 is the document number. You wrote that, Mr. Thornberry. And we said very precisely that we would not return fire whatever happened, that we would react only if they launched an offensive, which is something we would have to do then, and we were asking that a liaison officer from SpaBat be at HVO HQ or the operative zone in the area. Do you remember that now that we discussed that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that we were told that our -- our safety could not be guaranteed if we went beyond a certain line which I see now is described as the cease-fire line. And I've also indicated that we understood, everybody in the room understood, what that meant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, but on the second page there, it says that the BH army provides security. And my second question to you is this: Did you know that the Serbs or, rather, the army of Republika Srpska at that time was still shelling Mostar, whether East or West Mostar? Did you know that at least?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. So security provided by one side. When they say we're not going to return fire you're safe on our side. Now when the Serbs are going to shoot or the BH army would launch an attack using your -- and it says in one document -- in your document it says that they used your presence to transport units to the other side, but we won't go into that now. So can you confirm, one, that during your stay there from the HVO positions there was absolute peace? And we're going to see this on the tape that I'm going to show you. That there was complete peace and quiet, that there was no return fire, that there was no shooting, and that a SpaBat liaison officer was at the HVO headquarters in the operative zone throughout as somebody who was there to be a controller, to control our clear-cut options and the guarantees that we provided? Do you know that? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of it, no. What I was aware of was that there was still, from time to time -- let me begin that again. I'm sorry. I want to get this precisely. We knew from our experience there that at various points of time in the two or three days that we were there living in -- in the main street, we were -- we were well aware that from time to time there were likely to be outbreaks of fighting. And I believe, though I don't remember this in detail, this is the difficulty after this number of years, I believe that that was what was understood, and that certainly we behaved with considerable caution and prudence when we -- in particular when we exposed ourselves at various points in the street, in that main street. That's what I remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thornberry. Now, I'd like to round off a topic that wasn't dealt with completely, and that is the taking in of wounded by the HVO, something that you launched while you were there. That is to say that the HVO should enable the wounded to be pulled out of the hospital on the east side. So may we look at document P 05007.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: P 007. Yes. It's a document dated the 13th of September, 1993. The 13th we're talking about here, the 13th of September. Point 3. Let's just read what was done until that date. "Despite the successful evacuations to Zenica, another 41, which means a total of 160 so far." Now, can you confirm or do you remember that by the 13th of September a total number of wounded persons from East Mostar were transported to Zenica, Turkey, Croatia, and so on, a total of 160 patients were transferred?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it was so many, and I am very glad.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. That remained unclear. And then the operation continued. But up until the 13th, we managed to transfer these people, 160 of them, despite all the technical problems. Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you something about the water and electricity situation in Mostar. They said that there was no water in Mostar. We have heard about that. But, Mr. Thornberry, you at the time, you were there. Did you ask yourself any logical questions: Why was there no water in East Mostar? Who was to blame for that situation? Where was the water turned off if the HVO turned it off? What was the pipe situation? So taking the water from the source. So these technical questions that you would have to look at when there was a water shortage or no water somewhere. I'm asking you about this because the first reactions were there was no water in east water [as interpreted] it's -- the HVO is to blame. There's no electricity in East Mostar, the HVO is to blame. So my question is did you ask the people around you there was this water problem in East Mostar why was there this problem? Who was to blame, what had lapped to the pine lines and so on? I understand that you occupied a very high post, Mr. Thornberry, and you couldn't deal with all these details, these minor points, however, the reports do say no water in East Mostar, the HVO is to blame. So I'm wondering whether you asked any of these technical questions. Who was to blame for there being no water in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told by the local officials that there was no water, that water had to be taken from the Neretva, that although it was already polluted because there were no other adequate means of disposal, and that that situation continued for some time. In other words, very limited water carried around in buckets or whatever other containers there might be. This is what we were told. This is what I observed, that we were warned very solemnly by the doctors in the hospital not to use the water unless it was boiled thoroughly. I think that's the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are not answering the question that has been asked to you, and I could have asked it myself, because this question is at the very core of our concerns, and it is something that is referred to in the indictment. You're being told, "We have to go and get the water in the Neretva River." Doctors tell you the water has to be boiled. Fine. Very well. But the substantial question is why was the situation taking place? Who was preventing water from reaching the area? Who was preventing the electricity system from working? That's the question. Irregardless of -- of the problem, what was the reason for that problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this distance, sir, I cannot pretend that I know who turned the water off or who destroyed the pipes that brought water into the main part of the town. I don't know. I'm sorry, I forget. But it is not a -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the time you were probably one of the highest UN representatives there given your position within the UN administration. You're being told there is no water. People have to use the water from the Neretva River. Didn't you wonder why, why there was no water? I'll give you another example. In this very courtroom we -- we had problems. People were getting sick and so on. It came from the air-conditioning system. We didn't only say, okay, we're sick and we're cold. We try, we try and find out what was the cause of the problem. So you're being told in Mostar there's no water, there's no electricity. How come you didn't try to determine what was the cause of the problem? Because as you know, water is treated. You know that there are power plants to produce electricity. So these -- these are questions which need an answer. I understand you may not have an answer, but in this case please indicate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have an answer, but it's not perhaps too difficult to imagine how water or electricity would flow in a city in the condition in which Mostar was at that time. I think I have made the point elsewhere that Mostar was, in my personal opinion, it was in a worse condition, and that meant, inter alia, for utilities, water, electricity. Much worse than anything than I had seen in Sarajevo, for example, or in Vukovar. I -- you were kind enough to refer to me as a very senior official. I was. I was probably the most senior official in the United Nations for a hundred miles or anywhere around, but that doesn't -- I'm afraid, didn't give me automatic access to information. If I speak now about it, I would add just to this that I think that the -- I'm pretty sure I heard about the water and the electricity while I was there, but I do not remember the detail of it, unfortunately. I wish I did, but I don't. I can't invent it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You say you don't remember. Were you told in East Mostar, on the east side, that from the 30th of June four large hydroelectric power plants upstream from Mostar to Jablanica, that is Jablanica, Grabovica, Mostar 1 and Mostar 2, were totally under BH army control, these four large hydroelectric power plants after the 30th of June? And then the next question following on from that would be why did East Mostar not have no electricity when it had had enough power to light up a town of a million and a half inhabitants? So anybody who was with you or you yourself, did you wonder? Did you ask yourselves that question?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I speak only for myself and I don't have an answer to it, but I would have to say that I assumed, being not very skilled in these matters, that there was a good reason for there not being electricity, there was a good reason for not having water, there was a good reason for women scurrying across open spaces and being attacked by snipers. These were the kinds of things that in the daily business of running an operation you have to take for granted and then move on. If -- if we were not able to take it for granted, then we would have to find some other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me. Your Honour, do forgive me. On two occasions now the witness has been asked questions on this very important point, and in fairness to the witness in relation to Your Honour's question, he did say he couldn't answer, but he imagined, and he gave a scenario. Your Honour, once again he's asked a very straightforward question, and he says well, he supposes there's a good reason. I think it would help the Court to know, well, what was the good reason he thought. These are critical issues for anyone with an ounce of compassion nevermind a very senior, very respected United Nations official. They deal with water, electricity and the plight of civilians and to say that he imagines a good reason doesn't help us move matters forward an awful lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Without going into speculations you say you suppose there might have been a good reason, but you didn't know that there were four power plants which apparently from the month of June and onwards were under the control of the ABiH. If such power plants were under the control of the ABiH, the electricity going towards Mostar, if it was cut at the level of the power plants, well, the cause of the situation is the ABiH, not the HVO. On the other hand if power plants send electricity towards Mostar and if some people cut the pipes or do something to prevent electricity from reaching the city then it might be somebody else's fault. But I get the impression from your answers that you're not in a position to actually answer the question. Did you actually -- of course you said that you actually observed people running, that there was shooting, that some people were going to get some water in the river but the real cause behind the situation or the real causes you didn't try and find them, right?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the army -- pardon me. There was the army on the other side of the Neretva which did not cease for very long with respect to the -- to our colleagues which did not very long abstain from shooting at people who crossed the old bridge, for example. There was a particular difficulty in Mostar that the boundary line incorporated a part of West Mostar -- or was it the other way round? Incorporated part of the other side around the region of the bridge, the old bridge which has now been rebuilt. And indeed that was where some of the most unattractive conduct of the authorities in West Mostar, that was where they took place, these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. You are going a bit astray. I'm -- it's me who asks you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're going a bit astray. You were asked several times, repeatedly, whether you had any knowledge about the reasons why electricity and water were not available in East Mostar. You have volunteered imagination and suggestions, but isn't the fact that you simply do not know the reasons for either the water shortage or the shortage of electricity? You just know the fact of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is so, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thornberry. I certainly do agree with you that the problem of electricity supplies and water supplies in wartime is very problematic, and I know that not a day goes by when a shell doesn't hit a pipeline of some kind. All I was asking was no water, HVO to blame. No electricity, HVO to blame. Now, let's just look at something you mentioned here several times, the ruins of East Mostar. So let us look at 3D 01057, which was already shown here, and if it's on e-court, may we have it? My first question is this: Did you know that in Mostar in 1992 there was a very difficult war between, first and foremost, HVO units and the Yugoslav People's Army? Did you know about that? Did you know that in the spring and summer of 1992, to all intents and purposes, the BH army had taken control of East Mostar -- I'm sorry I misspoke. The Yugoslav People's Army, not the BH, the JNA and that it expelled the population and that it took control of parts of the hills above West Neretva? Did you know about that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So when you arrived in Mostar and you saw a town that had been as destroyed as Vukovar, did you ask yourself about the ruins in East Mostar and West Mostar, did you ask yourself how this came about? Through the shelling done by the HVO perhaps, or were the buildings destroyed from JNA shelling and torching? Perisic's units these were because General Perisic was the commander of those units in that area. Did anybody tell you about that, tell you of those facts?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably did, but I don't know from my own knowledge who, which side, which of the combatants was responsible for -- for these things. There is one other point that I ought quickly to make it. Going back if I may for a moment, before we left Medjugorje, all of us stocked up on bottled water, and we had enough water for drinking, in any event, for the four or five days, or three or four days when we were there. I had forgotten about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry -- Mr. Thornberry, my time's almost up, and I'm sure you're tired, too, so let's try and simplify this. My question was a simple one. We're going to take a look at the document. May we have the document put on e-court. And could you go through some of the images there? Can we look at the images, the footage. Take them in order, please, one by one. 3D 01057. 3D 01057 is the document number. And now let's just see the photographs. Here we have the first one. That's by the old bridge. By the old bridge. I'm going to ask you what year this happened. The second photograph is this. That's the hotel which was called Hotel Neretva, the Neretva Hotel in Mostar. Picture three, please. That's the old baths by Tito's bridge. Photograph four. That's the house next to the baths house. It's a musical school. It had been burnt down. You had to see whether it had been torched or burnt down in some other way. Could we please move on. That's Tito street. That's the main road, the main street that you yourself took. Let us stop here. Sir, do you know that these photographs were taken in the early fall of 1992? This was taken in 1992, in the early fall a book was published, the "Urbicide in Mostar." Could you please look at the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, perhaps to save time one could await the answer of the witness to your question. Because I do not think that two pictures more would make much difference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're perfectly right. It won't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So my question is as follows: According to a book that was published jointly by Croats and Muslims in 1992, it's call "The Urbicide," a claim is made that 90 per cent of Mostar, particularly the east part of Mostar, Mahala and so on, was destroyed by heavy artillery. It was set on fire, too, by the Yugoslav People's Army and the reservists who had come in from Montenegro. First there was the shelling, and then when the people fled the east side, and when they retreated in the face of our counter-attack they set everything on fire. For God's sake, did anyone give you those facts in Mostar? If not, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I've seen these photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am drawing to a close, but if this is the time for the break, perhaps it would be a good time to do it -- to do it now so Mr. Thornberry can rest a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, ideally it would be better to finish now. If there is no redirect, then the witness could leave and we can bring in the next witness. Could you just proceed quickly and put clear-cut questions to the witness so that we can finish now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, it is my intention to lead some redirect. It will be brief, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's let Mr. Praljak finish before the break, then, that he finishes his cross-examination, and then we'll have the redirect after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we please go back to 4D 00736 that I have asked to be prepared. This is a document from Bosnia and Herzegovina army where Sok Busic [phoen], and you were there at the time. The commander of the 6th Corps orders in the first paragraph: "Do not allow any movement of UNPROFOR, the ICRC, the UNHCR, and other international organisations, and prohibit the movement of any foreign journalists without the written approval of the corps commander." I'm waiting for the document to come up, but in the meantime as we're waiting for the document to come up, let me ask you whether anyone ever told you that the BH army, in this case it was the 6th Corps in Jablanica, at the time while you were there, expressly prohibited the movement of any vehicles of any international organisation?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might have done, but I'm not aware of it. It can't have been too significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can I ask which binder or where this exhibit can be located, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I can explain. General Praljak's Defence thought that this document would be in our binder, in General Petkovic's binder. Unfortunately, at the last minute we changed the way in which we intended to cross-examine, so we left it out. So you don't have it in hard copy. So could we please just all refer to the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You were not aware of that at any rate. Did you hear of it? Did anyone from UNPROFOR ever told you about that, about this ban on the movement of vehicles, at least as far as the 6th Corps is concerned. Jablanica, Konjic, that was the area covered by this corps of the BH army. And it is indicated here all the locations where the ban was in force, but I would like to speed this up. I don't want to bother you any more with that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite likely at that we were told about that. I -- I cannot be sure, and I cannot be certain, that's for sure. No. I don't remember where it comes from. I mean I know where it comes from. I don't remember its substance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I would just like to refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, the order is dated 29th of August, 1993, is sent by the 6th Corps to all its units as well as to UNPROFOR as I can see. It is stipulated that UNPROFOR should not move about, the ICRC and UNPROFOR, without a written permission from the 6th Corps. Theoretically you must have been made aware of this, because the UNPROFOR was one of the recipients of this order. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 29th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no memory of this at all. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, let me read out the number of the document. You don't have to go looking for it. It's P 04358. It's a report, Geneva, the 20th of August, and so on. And at one point, at the bottom of the first page, it says -- or, rather, I'm misquoting. At the beginning the first page it says: "A UN convoy that was under escort was turned back by the HVO immediately before crossing the river..." I don't know about that. "...on route to east Muslim sector where 35.000 people are living." Since one of the problems that we're facing now is how many people actually lived in this enclave there, what indicators were used by the people from any international agency, so this is within your purview, were used to come to an estimate as to the number of people who lived on the east bank of the Mostar river, to the south and to the north? So how did people learn of the number of people, because we have 35.000 people here, elsewhere we have 50.000, 30.000, 45.000. So I'm interested in the method of learning facts that was applied here, because this is what's killing us all, the ease with which apparently people learn facts.

Well, I haven't learned any. Not about this anyway. I don't know what the answer to this is. This is not only X number of years ago, it is also -- in my case I simply don't know how -- how we measure people. It's perfectly -- it's regrettable but factual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have one more question before we finish. We need to finish now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, perhaps we still have this problem of the ultimatum that is mentioned here. Perhaps I would take a couple of minutes more to do that, but at the bottom of the page in the same document it says that on Thursday the UNHCR reported that the situation in the Croatian part was really bad and on this basis we can assume what the situation is like in the Muslim part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it true, as far as you were able to see, that the situation as far as the water, food and electricity was concerned was very bad in West Mostar, too, while you were there?
I believe I remember learning that it was not quite as bad. I think they had power, for example. I don't know how, but I think they had power. I don't remember about water.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, if -- if I can be allowed just to show P 01299, the Kiseljak BH command. That's in the Prosecution binder. P 01299. The date is the 25th of January, 1993 and could we please look at paragraph 4(A), 4(A). This is all very short. 4(A), BritBat sector, British Battalion. And then in paragraph (A) it says Travnik, Novi Travnik. The situation has been very tense throughout the week. Some serious incidents have occurred during the past few days. The HVO ordered the Bosnian in Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez to hand over their weapons by 2400 hours on the 19th of January, 1993." So claim is made that by 2400 hours on the 19th they were supposed to hand over their weapons according to this famous ultimatum that we've heard so much about here. But it says -- goes on to say: "The order was later withdrawn by the HVO on the 20th of January, 1993." Are you aware of the fact that on the 20th of January this huge problem that arose from the so-called ultimatum ceased to exist, that this was all withdrawn, that this unfortunate piece of paper was withdrawn and was no longer valid at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to raise the objection I raised previously in cross-examination by other counsel. This is prior to the time of the witness's testimony, and it's also outside of the scope of the Trial Chamber's order which relates to Mostar. So I think both in time, in geography, this is beyond the scope of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Stringer is right, but the Trial Chamber may, at the request of -- I believe my colleagues don't agree with me. The witness was about to provide us with an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand, Your Honours, whatever your decision might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Trial Chamber feels that the question cannot be put unless the witness would like to respond spontaneously. Please, you have the floor, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should it be relevant, I wasn't actually in the mission area during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we shall --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much Mr. Thornberry. I understand the argument proffered by the Prosecution. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 4.00. We are going to have a 20-minute break and resume when we shall address the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Greetings, Mr. Thornberry. I've just got a couple of follow-up questions to ask you and then we'll be finished with your evidence.
[Overlapping speakers] -- qualification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The first question relates to something you were just talking about a couple of minutes ago on the cross-examination by General Praljak about the possibility that the electricity plants to the north had been taken over by the -- the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in response, part of your answer you indicated that you didn't have access to all of the information that was out there on that, and I wanted to use that to ask you in general to what extent did you and those around you in Mostar in those days have access to all that was happening, information to all that was happening on the ground militarily, both military activities of the HVO and the Armija and the extent to which those activities may have been affecting the things you were trying to do.

Well, we were at the mercy largely of information that was coming from Mostar to New York and then back again, and upon the decision of our colleagues in New York what was and was not relevant. So that was -- that was at times a very limiting factor. We were also receiving information back from some other duty stations in other places. On the whole, I think the information we were receiving, to be quite fair, was quite diligently presented, and the senior people of the United Nations secretariat were very active indeed they -- in seeing President Tudjman and many of the other senior personnel. One thing which was not included and which I haven't seen written about anywhere, was that at one point when things were getting rather unpleasant, somebody somewhere sent us three F-16s, I think they were, which buzzed up and down above the main street and made it -- made their -- their presence quite clear and significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me. I should have been more precise in my question, because you're clearly and correctly describe the access to information provided to you by people within the United Nations. I was actually -- I should have -- I should have asked it this way: To what extent did you have access to the information about the military activities of the HVO at the time? What were they doing there in Mostar as well as other places?
We didn't have any -- we didn't really have any -- any contact with the -- with them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was it the same for the Armija in terms of access to information of their's, what they were doing at any given time?
I think possibly more. More information of that kind was coming to us. We had very good relations all around, but I think the Armija was quite clearly had -- had an upper hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during the cross-examination by counsel for General Petkovic, Ms. Alaburic, she showed you a document that related to a shelling incident in West Mostar when some children were killed and wounded. Do you remember seeing that document?
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you -- well, if -- let me just -- let me just put it to you this way rather than taking the time to go back to the document, which was dated the 3rd of September, 1993. I just want to take you to another one which I don't have in the courtroom, which I ask that they put up on the e-court which is Exhibit P 4778, because this is also dated the same date, 3rd of September, 1993. 4778. I'm hoping we can get the translation on the e-court as well. There it is. Now, I don't expect you to have seen this before. This is a document that indicates it's an order to attack, and it's being issued on the 3rd of September by an HVO military commander. And I just show this to you to ask you to comment on this issue regarding negotiations with warring parties, what they say and what, on the other hand, might be happening in the field, and the extent to which you accept as true or as genuine representations that are made by warring factions in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the document in B/C/S on one side and in English on the other side, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the record, I would like to object to this question. Not so much to the question itself but to the document that is supposed to serve as the foundation for the question, because this is an order from the commander of the operation zone North-west Croatia -- Herzegovina. I do apologise. So this is the territory that does not include Mostar, and the cross-examination focused on Mostar. I don't think it is proper to extend the topic to include other zones in redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's -- it's -- I don't think there's any dispute that the witness was asked a lot about what the ABiH was doing and its effect on the negotiations and the activities of Mr. Thornberry. Now, we have heard that allegedly the Armija had taken control over some power plants that were up toward the Jablanica region as well. So in fact these are not issues which have been limited to Mostar. And I don't think that's relevant. I think the point is that the witness has been asked about Armija activities, and I think it's fair in redirect to ask him about HVO activities as well. In the context of the negotiations, which is the point of my question. I don't expect the witness to know about any specific attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just note one thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 3rd of July -- or, rather, the 3rd of September. This is after the events we've heard about, the events in Mostar. And second of all, this is a whole different area. This is the area around Prozor, as my colleague pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honour, Mackovac is a small area around close to Gorni Vokuf and Uskoplje, and there was intense fighting there for the reasons that were indicated earlier. Positions -- it changed hands very quickly. It has nothing do with power plants, Mostar. I could discuss that with another witness for hours. Mackovac is small hill close to Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Explain yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. September 3rd, Ms. Alaburic showed the witness a document from September 3rd as well which was one in which it indicates that shelling in West Mostar killed some children and injured some children. I think the point here is to go to the same day and to point out whether the HVO is engaged in military activities as well. The point was raised by counsel from General Petkovic in respect of the impact of the shelling activity on attempts to carry out these medical evacuations that were being attempted in early September of 1993. That's not just Mostar. It's Nova Bila as well, which is way up in Central Bosnia, and so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To sum up, to sum up, the Defence presented a document dated September the 3rd indicating that the ABiH carried out an attack in West Mostar. Now you're presenting an HVO document dating the same day, which provides for a military attack. Not in Mostar but elsewhere, and you want to establish a parallel, indicating that both forces, despite the discussions that were under way, that both forces were fighting. Am I correct? Okay. Well, then put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness -- I defer to counsel who is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I showed this document, not Ms. Alaburic. Despite your order to Mr. Stringer to continue, I would just like us to remind ourselves of the context. I showed this document precisely because I wanted to show that the BH army obstructed the implementation of this agreement about evacuation of the sick from East Mostar. I didn't want to use it in this broader context, and this is why I think that exhibiting those documents that refer to this whole area is completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
