utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's wait and see the question to be put to the witness. We are anticipating. We don't know what question will be put to the witness, and I don't know the answer either. So please put your question to the witness Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, you've see the document and you've heard the discussion of the other document which was shown to you by counsel for Mr. Stojic. And I apologise to counsel for the mistake. The point of the questioning is this -- and actually let me introduce maybe another remark or a point that was raised by the President when he was commenting on the video that was shown of the meetings in Medjugorje which the HVO -- my question is this. If you could comment on someone who has been a negotiator at these levels, cordiality as was indicated on the tape, things that are said in negotiations versus events on the ground, and to what extent you had access to military activities, and comment on how that could have effected, then, your ability to carry out your mandate in these negotiations?
I'm sorry, I'm not sure that I understand what is being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question is this: In negotiations, even those that are being conducted in a cordial atmosphere, do you accept at face value representations and statements made by warring factions?
Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you have access to -- are you privy to information about military activities that are being carried out perhaps at the same time by those warring factions?
It does happen. It depends on a number of factors, including where you are and -- and at what stage and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next question relates to the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, could we see that video again, because I believe it's quite enlightening, the video where we see the witness meeting with other officials, but he's not of course the only one. There are also UNPROFOR members present. Could we see that video again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just reach for my notes and I can get the number for Ms. Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very brief. I think it's only two minute long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: "Welcome. Very good to see you. Please come through. You know Shannon Boyd. "[Inaudible] Interpreter: "Hello. "Did you find the interpreter? "Yeah, we did. "[Indiscernible] Thank you very much indeed, General. Thank you. "General, I want to introduce my -- the new commander. We come here. [Indiscernible]. "Mr. Albert Benabou. Okay. "Okay. Very good. All right. "Thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, that is Exhibit P 02950. I should say also that the other two clips are also the same exhibit which is P 04296.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And witness, and I know I'm asking this inartfully, but we have the images there. At the same time we have a war going on. And the question is you're approached in negotiations in this context then, whether the words and the views expressed in these negotiations then would be accepted by you and whether you approached them differently.

The -- the manner of speaking on the part of the two parties there, the United Nations on one side and the MOAT -- the MOAT on the other is absolutely characteristic of -- if one in fact did not communicate and slap the back of and all that kind of thing, it would be regarded as being a false -- something false. It can be taken to extremes, but they are de rigeure really is what it comes down to, and I have once or twice in my lifetime been simply unable to shake the hand of someone who is on the other side, but those are extremely rare events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You testified on cross-examination that the source of information about the targeting of civilians in East Mostar was the surgeons, I believe you indicated.
The source of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you have any other sources who -- on the issue of targeting civilians in East Mostar apart from those -- those -- the Bosnians who were living in East Mostar?
Well, there was -- of course there was Colonel Morales who was shown on the -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's what I was getting at actually. Were any internationals also a source of information on that?

Well, Colonel Morales was a source of a great deal of information, and a very competent and experienced colonel, and he, of course, had been brought in fairly recently into the area, and he had been -- he had actually been briefed by many of the same people who briefed me also, because although I was just a given, technically speaking, in this international peacekeeping the lines become -- become -- military and civilian, become somewhat blurred at times, and in crisis very blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. In his cross-examination, General Praljak showed you photographs of the east side of Mostar from the 1992 conflict with the Serbs. Do you recall that?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You don't have to go to the document although you can if you wish. It's P 4673, 4673, which is in your binder there, which you testified about yesterday. This is your 1 September 1993 memo to Mr. Stoltenberg.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And right at the beginning of it you said that you had met with civilian and military leaders of East Mostar yesterday evening. "East Mostar had been pounded with artillery and mortar for many hours that day."
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So my question is do you recall then during this latter half of August, was East Mostar the target of -- of shelling activity?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you know which of the parties was shelling East Mostar during that time?
Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.
I could make a guess, but it wouldn't be a useful guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were asked questions yesterday about the media campaign that was organised in respect of the trip, the first trip to East Mostar. Actually, I'm finished with the document now, so I'm moving on to the next question. My question is this, Mr. Thornberry -- excuse me. You don't need to read the document any more. I've got the answer for that last question. The next question is about the media campaign, and you were asked questions about the impartiality which was involved in that, and the one question I had for you on that is in making that media campaign and in showing the images that were shown, did you approve or intend that any of the images or any of the information was to misrepresent --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my learned friend is -- knows very well that the proper question, of course, is to ask what was intended. Leading questions are not appropriate in re-examination as they're not appropriate in examination-in-chief, and the witness is highly intelligent. He doesn't need to be spoon fed in this rather blatant manner in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't think that's a leading question, Mr. President, but I'll abide by whatever decision obviously the Trial Chamber takes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Just rephrase your question. Make sure that it is a broad question that the witness can answer. When I put a question, for instance, there are several possible answer. I never hint at an answer. So please try and put the question to him in such a way that he can answer it, and then you can go into the detail of that subject by asking a follow-up question to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, the question is about the media campaign, and you testified that the intent or the desire was that it generate a response to the international community. The question is, then, what was your approach to the information that was to be included in that media campaign?

Under normal circumstances, I would expect to see the text of a draft document, for example, before anyone else other than the author of it became -- moved on. It's difficult to -- it's difficult for me to understand exactly what counsel may be reaching for in this question, because the relation -- it is not really a media campaign, quote and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I think that you did not understand the question that was put to you by Mr. Stringer. You told us that in order to convey the mission, in order to convey the idea of what you were doing on the ground, you decided to visit on a number of occasions certain parts of that region, and you decided that you would be accompanied by television crews, and this is what we saw a while ago. We saw you and somebody had shot that film. We see you meeting with the HVO. So Mr. Stringer is putting the question to you, but when this kind of campaign is underway, how can you control all of this? How can you make sure that you are still aware of the message that is going out to the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we are in fact controlling the information which is contained in this "campaign." I wouldn't use that term myself, perhaps, because it suggests a rather broad detailed document such as we were looking at a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. How do you control that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you control it at source. You -- I mean, this is what fact gathering by an international organisation who is -- which is in an operational situation, this is the kind of thing which they're supposed to -- to deal with, and some of us have also been journalists at some point or other in our misspent youth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is your case, I believe. You were a journalist in the past, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are an expert, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, was the President's question that the witness was an attorney or a journalist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Journalist, journalist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, you don't usually go to the press with a story until you have authenticated it and checked it out essentially politically. Whether it -- if it's in fact a United Nations document, is it going straight down the middle. Are you in fact being adequately objective in a situation in which feelings and experiences may run very high and very hot. I can't really -- I've done it many, many times. I think most of us who work in the political upper reaches of the Secretariat of the United Nations are very familiar with the necessities of those -- that situation. I'm not sure that I'm responding to you, sir, but I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll just follow up with one last question on this. What you -- what you just said, Mr. Thornberry, is that you don't usually go to the press with a story until you have authenticated it and checked it out. So the question then would be: In respect of this media campaign that you've testified about, are you confident that that was authentic.

Yes, I think it was authentic. It was a little bit -- it was a little bit too long to be effective would have been my response at that time. And I probably wasn't able to find the author of the story in any event because I was probably in some other place in movement, and that situation was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. My last question relates to an exhibit that was shown to you, or whether you were asked about, I should say, by counsel for General Petkovic, and that is the transcript of a tape-recorded meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's Exhibit 4D 00930. And you don't have to turn to it, Witness, but there is a reference here to a meeting, or I should say there is a reference to the Croatian foreign minister, Mr. Granic, whom you've testified about, and I wanted to ask you one thing from this transcript and ask you if you could comment on it. I'm at page 14 of the English version. Someone named Haris Silajdzic is talking, and he says: "I pointed out -- I pointed that out to Granic during the talks in Vienna. He says, you know, that we expect that after two years of European Union administration Mostar becomes the capital of Herceg-Bosna." Now, my question, Mr. Thornberry, is whether in all of your dealings and negotiations with Mr. Granic, he ever expressed a view that Mostar would be the capital of Herceg-Bosna?
Not publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did he do so privately?
It sounds very familiar, but I -- I would not want to be absolutely categorical. I think I know when it comes -- what it comes from, but I'm not completely sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, after having testified for three days, I would like to thank you for having come, and I wish you well in your future endeavours and in your current job, and I wish you a safe journey home. I would like to thank you. And I would like the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, before we hear the next witness, I have two decisions to hand down. Our time is precious, and I like to do as best I can. Oral decision pertaining to the admission of evidence tendered through Witness EI. I'm going to check the English translation at the same time. The Trial Chamber is handing out a decision on the matter of the admission of evidence presented to Witness EI, who appeared before the Trial Chamber on the 10th of January, 2008. It admits the evidence P 10210 under seal, and P 10211 under seal presented by the Prosecution through its list IC 00771. It also admits Exhibit P 09440, presented by the Defence of Mr. Coric through its list IC 00772. These exhibits, in the Chamber's view, do have a certain reliability, relevance, and probative value. So let's move into private session now, please, because we need to hand down a decision in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you Your Honours. It's short simple application and I'll be as quick as I can. It's an application for the hearing of a preliminary issue and what I'll do, Your Honours, first is say what we propose the preliminary issue should be and then indicate what we have to say about the suggested practicalities. It's -- it's relatively short. It is to -- the issue is what powers does the Trial Chamber have, A, under Rule 98 bis or alternatively, B, under Rule 54 to strike out a discrete material allegation included under any one of the 26 counts in the indictment on the ground that there is no evidence capable of supporting that allegation, notwithstanding that the Trial Chamber does not enter a judgement of acquittal on that count under Rule 98 bis. Now, Your Honours will see that language that bit of language in the middle, there is no evidence capable of supporting that allegation is lifted from Rule 98 bis, but the point being that where this applies not to every allegation in a particular count but only to some, but we do qualify it by referring to them as discrete material allegations. Your Honour -- Your Honours, this -- an answer to this question would be very important to set the fundamental guidelines for the substantive application that under the current Scheduling Order Your Honours have in mind to begin on Monday, the 28th of January. Now, Your Honours, what we suggest is that it would be extremely valuable to the Trial Chamber, in fact, with respect, but also to the parties to have an answer to that question. Now, of course to some extent the practicality depends -- Your Honour, I -- Your Honour just -- something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to answer on the legal matter, and then if you wish you can address the practicalities at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I straight away before Your Honour does that, it's absolutely -- I notified Mr. Stringer that I would be making this application so that we didn't spring it on them unexpectedly today, but I have assured him, and I rather think it's his position but he can speak for himself, but I wasn't proposing to argue anything today on the -- the substance of that preliminary issue. It's absolutely not my intention to argue anything, and I was not inviting, and with respect, was rather disinviting the Trial Chamber from any expression or any point of view. That's for the hearing of the preliminary issue, but perhaps I ought just to have added that Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, you're raising the issue of Rule 98 bis. I'd like now to give you my personal opinion, not the opinion of my colleagues. I was part of the Plenary meeting when the decision to alter this rule was taken, so I can give you an informed contribution. As you know, this is a common law rule. At the beginning there were a lot of written decisions. Each time there was a particular application on Rule 98 bis, parties would provide submissions, written submissions, and then this would be followed by an oral procedure. This was taking a lot of time, and sometimes the decisions rendered by Trial Chambers could be a hundred pages and more. Aware of that problem, Judges decided to amend that Rule and to amend it on the basis of a proposal made by a common law Judge who explained how the whole thing worked. He explained to his fellow Judges that in his own jurisdiction, in his own country, at the end of the Prosecution case, this is how things would work, the Defence was allowed to step in and say that the Prosecutor, on a particular charge of the indictment, did not provide enough evidence and then the Judge would decide whether the application should be dismissed or agreed, adopted. This was a very quick way of dealing with this matter, and of course it was very convincing for all the Judges within the Tribunal, and that's why there was a new Rule 98 bis which allows such procedure to take orally. You will have noted that Rule 98 bis does not talk any more about charges, counts, which means that the discussion will focus on counts. The issue at stake for a particular Chamber is that for a particular count, let's take the example of persecution, the Chamber will have to decide whether the Prosecution was able to show enough evidence proving that there had been persecution. And if there is one piece of evidence, because there is a minimum standard set in that Rule, then there is no acquittal and the proceedings will continue. This is how things should work. As everybody else I studied what had happened in other Chambers to see how in practice things worked and of course practices varied. In some cases Defence counsel decided to deal with various paragraphs saying in paragraph 4, for instance, the Prosecution was not in a position to bring in any significant evidence, and then others dealt count by count saying for at that particular count there hasn't been any evidence, which means that with this very quick procedure, when the Defence takes the floor the Defence may say let's deal with it paragraph by paragraph or count by counsel, on that particular paragraph or count the Prosecution was not in a position to present enough evidence showing that there was indeed cases of persecution, but again this is an example I'm taking. Then the Prosecution will take the floor and say, "I have shown such document, P, X, Y, Z. I have shown this particular witness," and then will give you references to the transcript. And then after deliberation the Chamber will issue a decision. This is the letter and the spirit of the Rule 98 bis. I believe that in two cases, in two particular cases, I believe that the Prosecution case ended at 11.53 and at 12.53 in multiple accused case. The decision was rendered by the Chamber, i.e., less than an hour after. We have decided to wait for a few days before issuing our decision. This is all I can say. When the hearing will take place, for each different accused we have decided upon one particular day. That is, you have almost more than four hours to say whatever you want to say. Then the accusation will reply, and then we will issue our decision two weeks later. If you want to, you can deal with it paragraph by paragraph. You can deal with it count by count. But what I want to say is that a count may refer to several municipalities. For the count of destruction, it is enough for one municipality to have one document saying there was a case of destruction in that municipality for the counts to be kept, and then there will be no acquittal. This is the letter and this is the spirit. Mr. Stewart, I don't know if -- if I shed some light on this matter but this is what I am in a position to stay at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That has certainly shed some light on Your Honour's views by expressing them. There is no question about that. But may I observe two things. First of all, it is precisely these issues which we wish to argue and have the possibility of making submissions upon before there's a ruling, and Your Honour has very clearly and expressly stated that the views that you have just expressed are not the views of the Trial Chamber, were simply Your Honour's own views. Consequently we do not have, and that was our position, we didn't ask for a decision this afternoon in fact we've asked specifically not to have a decision because we wish to adopt, with respect, conventional old-fashioned approach of making submissions first and then inviting a decision on our submissions. So, Your Honour, what we wish to do is avoid the situation where this important issue is canvassed at the beginning of the substantive 98 bis application, then we go straight on to that application. We suggest that on this important issue it's much more satisfactory if we do have a clear ruling based on our argument from the Trial Chamber so that we know where we are with -- with at least some sort of a gap then before we return for the actual application. And, Your Honour, by the way, may I -- Your Honour, may I simply add one thing. It is it is my application, Your Honour that Rule 54 is expressly mentioned in our application. Nothing that Your Honour said a moment ago touched on Rule 54. It is extremely important to bear in mind that that Rule is there. It's often appealed to by the Trial Chamber as a general power, and we will argue and we do argue that quite separately as an alternative to 98 bis Rule 54 does offer the opportunity of proper discipline in relation to the situation contemplated in the preliminary issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, you're right. I gave you my personal opinion, because I took part in the exercise which led to the new version of Rule 98 bis. This is my own opinion. As regards the decision that will be made by the Chamber as a whole, this is something else. You will have one day, one day, to present your submissions. You'll have one day. You and the other member of your team, you will have the time to tell us what you want to say. We'll give you enough time for four hours. Four hours and a half. You will let us know what you want to say have to say. While you will be presenting your submissions we'll take notes as is usual. Then the Prosecution will have the opportunity to answer, and we will have two weeks to deliberate before we issue a decision, and it will it be an oral decision, which will be a response to your arguments, your submissions. So do not fear. Judge Trechsel would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will address you in your own language to avoid the necessity of interpretation. I'm not quite sure whether your query has actually been answered by the president. As I understand you, you are raising a question that goes slightly beyond Article 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you wonder whether, let's say, alongside a strict application of that disposition which speaks of charges, not accidentally but some way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of counts of counts of counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think in English it is -- whatever. We understand. One of the 26. Your -- your -- the question you want to raise is whether there is a possibility within these 26 points to extract not acquit but drop, as it were, certain elements in order to alleviate the weight of the further proceedings, and I -- I think this is a -- a question that is worth discussing. I'm not in any way taking a point on -- on the merits of it. I think it is something on which, of course, the Prosecution must also be heard, and I think we should probably not too late next week find a moment where we can have a session where we discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- Your Honour absolutely has the point spot on with respect, absolutely spot on, and that is exactly the point. I -- I need say no more, Your Honour, because what Your Honour said encapsulates the application I've made absolutely perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I'll add one thing. I limit myself to Rule 98 bis. I didn't mention Rule 54. This is a 98 bis procedure. That's my position. I saw somebody waving. Mr. Prlic maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. May I say for the record. I heard your decision. The ruling is as it stands, and my only reason was transparency for the proceedings, why I made the request. But let me just say that I'm not quite clear why your oral decision was made in public session, in open session. That's the first point. And secondly, I'm not quite clear about why in the court ruling announced in open session words are quoted which were uttered in closed session. And I'm also not clear on another point. It's not my Defence counsel who is being punished but me, why the parties weren't heard properly before this ruling was made. But I'm not asking for a new ruling. I'm saying all this in order to achieve my primary goal, which is complete transparency for these proceedings and that all the decisions and rulings of this Trial Chamber be consistent and proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for your intervention. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A very short commentary, Mr. Prlic. The decision is on -- on formal grounds, but as far as the substance is concerned, you may have noticed that the declaration made, I think on the 14th by your counsel, has been made in open session, and it gives quite a bit of information in fact. So the matter is not as sealed as you might fear. I think a certain transparency is apparent therefrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just two very brief, because we have a witness. Certainly if the Trial Chamber's going to consider the application that my learned friend Mr. Stewart has just described, the Prosecution will look forward to presenting its views on that. I'm not going so say anything more about that at that -- at this time. Clearly we want to be heard. It may be that if we find ourselves discussing the modalities of 98 bis, the Prosecution may, and I'm just going to mention this now, because I was -- actually, what interested me more was less the application and more the remarks of the president regarding the procedure in which it's apparently envisioned that the Defence makes a submission for any number of hours of length related to any number of the allegations and evidence that is included in this vast case, and then the Prosecution is expected to stand up and address those issues in a way that is viewed as -- as full enough to at least accurately present the Prosecution case. I don't know that we can do that, and it would be our request that we take all the Defence submissions on this orally in open court and that at -- after some break, after some passage of time, the Prosecution then has the opportunity to address those, which gives us time to prepare our submissions, which is what the Defence are doing right now. They have an advantage to prepare their submissions. We don't know what they'll be, and I don't know that it will be very helpful to the Trial Chamber to expect the Prosecution to then stand up immediately and to address any number of specific issues which we don't see coming. So we'll be asking -- and I'm not asking for any decisions now, just like Mr. Stewart's not asking for any decisions now, but it's something that we'd like to discuss further with the Trial Chamber if we're talking about this next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can help Mr. Stringer on this. Maybe -- I don't know about Mr. Khan, perhaps he's going to be helpful as well, he usually is, but we can help Mr. Stringer on this as far as the -- on the previous application I had the support of all my colleagues having discussed it with them. Here I'm just speaking for the Petkovic Defence, but we will provide the Prosecution with -- with some outline of the submissions that we propose to make. We do consider that to be good practice. We consider it to be helpful to everybody, and we will offer such a skeleton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, first of all I wish to say that as far as I'm concerned, and I'm speaking as a personal capacity, not on the behalf of my fellow Judges, I do not want to be manipulated in this 98 bis proceeding. There is a Rule in the Rules of this Tribunal. I've had in the past the opportunity to deal with that Rule, so I won't take any lessons. There are four Chambers, four Chambers. They issued decisions. Let me invite you to read those decisions, to read whatever was said by the Defence counsel as well as by the Prosecution teams on that particular procedure. Up to now there hasn't been anything revolutionary. It has always been very classical, traditional, so please do not make more complicated than it is, a specific procedure which has been working for years in this Tribunal, which has been working in written form, which has worked as well in oral proceedings. Some of you may have some experience, Mr. Karnavas among other Defence counsel, Mr. Kovacic, and others maybe, maybe others will have less experience in the matter. I'm also very surprised by what I've heard from Mr. Stringer, he's asking for more time. His colleagues in other trials were in a position to reply on the basis of what Defence counsel say. When you know a specific case, you're in a position to say on that particular count I have such-and-such documents which go in a different direction from what the Defence is arguing. Something else I haven't said. This procedure takes place on the basis of the evidence presented by the Prosecution and not by the Defence. Please keep this in mind. It was recalled in various decisions issued by other Chambers. However, the Chamber has heard Mr. Stewart, has heard Mr. Stringer. We will discuss this matter because I've only given you my own personal opinion. Maybe my colleagues will have another opinion. We will issue a decision which will either be unanimous or by majority. It is now 25 past 5.00. We need to bring the next witness in because the idea would be to proceed expeditiously and to finish with that witness by 7.00. There hasn't been any new information about this witness, so we'll have the witness brought in without further ado. My colleague is talking to me about a break. You know that I don't really like the word "break." It seems that a break is needed, so we will a have a 20-minute break. I wanted this witness to have him brought in so I completely forgot about the break, but we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. First of all could you stand up, please, because I would like you to take the solemn declaration. Please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kemal Likic, the 4th of January, 1953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you currently have an occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before a court on the events that took place in your country or is it the first time you testify today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I'm testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you read the text before you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. So I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution. The Prosecution is going to give us a brief summary, and I'd like the Prosecution to speed things up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'll try to be as expeditious as possible. I'll start with a brief summary of the witness's evidence taken from the 65 ter summary. The witness in this case was a Bosnian Muslim man from Stupni Do. In July 1992, he joined the Muslim guards of the village who had already organised themselves. They were supervised by Esref Likic. In a sketch attached to the statements given by him, the witness locates the trenches that were dug around the village to defend them against Serb and Croat attacks. He explains how the guards were organised. Potok was the most dangerous duty point. On the 23rd of October, 1993, when he returned from his guard duty, the attack on Stupni Do began.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One interpreter is enough. I don't need two. Let me repeat. There are two interpreters that are translating into French. I only need one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: He went home, put on his uniform, took his gun, and with his neighbour, Salko Likic, went towards the trench position on Bogos hill. On their way they were told by other guards about the death of two fellow guards at the Bogos hill trench. One of the victims was Salko Likic's son. Later, Salko's body was found near the place where his son had died. The rest were able to reach Ravasnica where they were involved in combat. After a while, two women from the village came to their position and told them that they were the only survivors of a group that had sought refuge with them. The Croatian Defence Council soldiers sent a message through the women ordering them to surrender. Some men went back to the village to try and help the villagers. The witness and others left in the direction of Strijezevo and at Pajtov Han where a Croatian Defence Council check-point was they had to hide. From their hiding point, the witness could see the roads and noticed a lot of movement. He saw a local camouflage painted Croatian Defence Council APC moving on the road making several rounds that day between Vares Majdan and Pajtov Han. On the road to Planinica he saw trucks carrying heavy arms. On Monday morning, 25th of October, 1993, the witness and other villagers went back to the village. At the place called Stanica, the witness saw the dead body of Zejnil Mahmutovic who was shot with a dum-dum bullet. He only entered the village at night and was accompanied by Dzafo Rasim. During the day he saw two soldiers drinking. When he arrived near his house he saw a burnt dead body which was afterwards identified as Merima Likic. His house had been burnt. In the basement he saw the massacred and mutilated bodies of Nevzeta Likic, Hatidza Likic and Medina Likic. The next morning the witness and other villagers were rescued by UNPROFOR. Three days later, UNPROFOR found five other burnt bodies in the witness's house, amongst them Merina Likic, Vahidin Likic, Mebrura, Likic Suhra, and Zukic Lejla. The witness knows that they were brought to the morgue. Later the burnt body remains of his son, Adis Likic, were found in the house. And that concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Likic, I just have a few questions for you and I would greatly appreciate if you could give me short answer unless I ask you to elaborate further. Firstly, did you provide written statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in connection with what happened in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that those statements were given on the 16th of March, 1998 -- 1996, and the 28th of October 1998 respectively?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the time you gave those statements, did you answer any questions the investigators asked you correctly and truthfully?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't understand that question, actually. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you speak the truth to the investigators when they asked you any questions? Were you answers correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you give the information freely and without any force or coercion?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of the two statements were your statements read back to you in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you remember did you sign and initial those statements?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, Your Honours, I'd like to show the witness the statements at this stage, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If you could turn firstly to P 10102 and to the Bosnian version. Do you recognise this as the statement that was given?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you look at the start -- at the English version, do you recognise the signatures appearing on the English version on the back page?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps if the usher would stay with him for the moment it would speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Last page of the English version. Do you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you turn then to the second statement, which is P 10074. Again if you look at the English version, do you recognise the signature and the initials appearing? And again are those your signatures and initials?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you recently confirm those statements again before a court officer before coming to this court?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you travelled to The Hague here a few days ago, did you meet with myself and an investigator, and did you review your statement?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you have any additions or alterations to make to the statement?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you had to give the evidence as contained in those statements over again, is what you said in the statements what you would tell us at the Court here today?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Starting with your first statement on the 16th of March, 1996, you told -- you said at the early stage that you were performing guard duty in the village of Stupni Do starting on the 1st of July, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you a part of a larger group of guards from the village?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Three soldiers. Three soldiers up at the trench, if I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did the village have a larger defence guard stationed in it? How many soldiers or how many guards were in your guard unit?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Forty-two or 43. I'm not quite sure. Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what was the average -- what was the average age of the members of this guard unit?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: From 18 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you uniformed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, which I personally bought.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did everybody have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what training did you receive within this guard unit to assist you in performing your duties?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: I did not attend any training.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did most of the members of the guard unit have some form of training from their time serving with the former Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How were you armed in your unit in 1992? What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: I had a Russian -- an old Russian automatic rifle manufactured in 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when the unit was formed initially, how many pieces of armaments did you have between your 42 to 43 people? How many rifles did you have?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: We had seven rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you receive some armaments from outside between July 1992 and the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: During this period was your unit, if we want to call it as such, taken over and did it fall within the umbrella of the Armija?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did the numbers on your unit stay the same in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell me in the latter part of 1993, in the period September/October, who was the commander of your unit?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: The commander was Himza Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sorry, could you say that name again for us?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: The commander was Himza Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Himza Likic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Himza.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did he remain as commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: He was commander until he was arrested by members of the Croatian Defence Council, their soldiers, seven days prior to the attack on Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And prior to the attack on Stupni Do, what was the position in terms of weapons that your unit possessed? You had got some weapons from the outside you told us. How many weapons did you now possess within your unit?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Twenty-eight barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what type of weapons were they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Three Russian automatic rifles, three M-48 rifles, semi-automatic, well, I don't know how many semi-automatic rifles there were, and two Kalashnikovs. That makes, I think, 28. I can't really say how many automatic rifles there were, but there were two Kalashnikovs, so 28 in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. For the sake of completeness, did your unit possess a mortar which it had received from the Armija?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I never saw it, nor did I ever hear that it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you described having been on guard duty on the night of the 22nd of October, 1993, and you were relieved by a shift, the other shift, in the morning of the 23rd of October. How long were these shifts?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: The shifts lasted 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in your statement you stated that you went home and that while having coffee with a neighbour the attack on Stupni Do started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you expecting -- were you expecting an attack on Stupni Do on this particular day?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what form did the attacks take? How did you know there was an attack starting? What did you see or hear?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: There was firing. The first shell was fired from the positions of the Croatian Defence Council at the positions of the BH army and the attack started with all available artillery weapons and infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you say the positions of the Croatian Defence Council, what positions were they occupying?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: The HVO positions were located at Bijelo Borje, the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was this the only position that fire was coming -- attack was coming from?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: There was another position from town, from Vares Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you stay in your statement that you put on your uniform and you made your way with another neighbour. You were attempting to go towards the Bogos trench and that you met a number of soldiers halfway up the hill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Had you fired at anybody at this stage? Had you seen any of the attackers?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We opened fire from the forest, and they were shooting when they took Bogos and moved towards the village of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'd like at this point in time if I may, I enclosed at the back of your booklet a number of photographs which don't, unfortunately, have exhibit numbers, but I enclosed them for the benefit of the Court, and I wonder if they could be put on the ELMO, starting with the first one, just to help us orientate ourselves. Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph? Is that the village of Stupni Do towards the centre?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the village of Stupni Do and the surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And is this a view of Stupni Do coming from the direction of Vares Majdan?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me take stock. No. No. Oh, just a minute. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If you see, there's a road running from the front of the photograph --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: To the right of Vares Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. Do you see the road running through the centre of the photograph from the front of the photograph towards the village?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is that the road leading from Vares Majdan into the village?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps if we turn to the second photograph it would be clearer. On the second photograph you see two roads running from the front of the photograph to the back. The road on the left, is that the road from Vares Majdan leading into the village?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Flynn. If you look at the first picture again, the previous one, you will see that the road which you have now identified as going to Vares is far -- or quite a bit to the left from the one we had first. It's the lower road.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That's right. I had asked him initially to identify the road in the middle of the photograph leading into Vares, which is the lower road, and that's why I showed him the second one. I think it's easier to determine it from the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So the lower road, the one towards the left of the photograph, is the one leading into -- into Stupni Do from -- from Vares Majdan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you see Bogos hill in that photograph, for the benefit of the Court?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No, you can't see it. You have to go a little further up this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In which direction, to the left or right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: The right. Towards the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you turn to photograph number three, this shows a side view, I believe of the village, with the road from Vares Majdan coming from the right into the centre of the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you see Bogos hill in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us if you can see it or approximate where you were positioned, where you had met your comrades often the hill who had told you that there were people killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, don't you think that it might be interesting to give a pen to the witness so that he can mark things on the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That's what I was in the process of about to say. I was asking him if he could indicate where he was, and then I was going to ask him if he could mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So again, Mr. Likic, could you indicate if you can see on the map where you were when you met your friends who had come from Bogos hill and could you mark it with an X.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell me were there any HVO forces on Bogos hill that you saw?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No. We did not manage to get to the Bogos hill because the HVO forces took them. This is where I put the mark "X."

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you see or hear any HVO forces on the hill? Were there any forces close to you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council forces, I didn't see them. They fired from the deciduous forest, and we returned fire from this position where I put the mark, which was a pinewoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know if the HVO forces were descending down the hill in the direction of where you were?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the position which you've marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: An hour and a half to two hours. I didn't have a watch, so I did indicate that I was giving a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And during that time did you happen to look back in the direction of Stupni Do, and if you did, could you tell the panel what you saw?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw the Bogos hill, the village, the road to Vares Majdan, the road to the Prica Do hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you see whether all the houses in the village were still intact?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a newly built village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But we're talking about on the day of the attack. When you looked back to Stupni Do, were the houses the same as they had been, for example, the day before?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you see any signs of any premises being on fire?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: First the barns were set on fire, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: When the Croatian Defence Council troops entered the village, the infantry, they started to torch the houses and kill the innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you see houses that were on fire?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them from up there where I was, the position that I marked with an "X."

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you told about your wife and another lady arriving up from the village having been sent to ask you to surrender. From that I understand that the -- that the HVO forces must have entered into the village. Is that -- was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's when the Croatian forces entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know from which direction the forces that entered the village would have come?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: From what I was able to see, from the direction of Vares Majdan and from the direction of Bijelo Borje village. And the forces that headed from Bogos were not able to go through, and they went to the Prica Do hamlet where they committed this crime, and they came in towards my house through this area here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would you make sure that you speak into the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you and accurately interpret what you're saying, please. When you say that committed this crime in the Prica Do hamlet, was this hamlet part of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what crime was committed there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I heard. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us in brief what crime was committed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, they killed Zejnil Mahmutovic, who was on guard duty, and then the women and the children, civilians, there were also some men there, they slaughtered them. They slit their throats. They slit the throats of the men, and they shot the rest into a small house, and they set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know from what you were told as to how many people at this particular location were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Ten people, I believe, ten people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you described in your first statement of the 16th of March, 1996, where your defensive trenches were situate, and these appear to have been situate outside the village of Stupni Do. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did your -- did your unit have a second --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did your unit have a second line of defence in the event that these trenches fell or were captured?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, if there were any strong points or bunkers or trenches situate within the village itself from which the unit could defend the village in the event that they had to leave the first line?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: There were a number of houses in the village with cellars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think your own house, for example, had a cellar.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was there any possibility that these cellars could be converted into a strong point or a bunker from which a defence could be operated or maintained?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No. My cellar, I used it to put the winter food stores, and this is where people took shelter when the village was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Remaining with your cellar, you told in your statement about coming back to the village and finding three women in the cellar who were dead. Can you tell us, was there anything in your cellar at the time -- was there anything in your cellar at the time that might have presented a danger to the HVO that would have justified them killing the people in the basement?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No. There was just the winter food stores, potatoes, onions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And as regards Stupni Do itself, just looking at the maps we see the road leading from Vares Majdan into the village, and if you go through the village the road comes out, I believe, on the other side and goes in the direction of the village -- the Croat village of Mir; is that correct? ?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did people from Mir use this road to get access from Vares Majdan and ultimately to the town of Maric?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they use it to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge during the summer of 1993 and leading up to the time of the Stupni Do attack, was there any attempt on the part of your unit to prevent any of the Croat population from the surrounding villages to use this road?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: During the period -- during the summer of 1993 leading up to the incident in Stupni Do, did any of your unit -- did you or any of your unit try to prevent your Croat neighbours from using this road?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you can think -- that you can think of why the -- your village should have been attacked by HVO on the 23rd of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: There was no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you said -- you told in your second statement, and I'm coming towards the end of my questions, you said in your second statement of the 28th of October, 1998, at the end that after the bodies of certain people which had been found and identified by UNPROFOR had been found, your son Adis, his body was later found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when Adis's body was found and where it was found?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: My son Adis, his body was found close to my family home, 15 to 20 metres away. There was some planks put up there for some construction work. This is where he was killed. Actually, he was wounded close by. His mother saw him there. He was wounded, and probably - I was not there - he was thrown onto this plank or board. He was either dead or still alive but wounded, and he was -- he burnt down there and his bones were found there and they were identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How was he identified, in what manner? Was it through his dental records or clothes or -- take your time.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: He was identified -- he was identified since he was the -- in the 19th generation of the police academy in Vraca. He was wearing military police-type boots when I got him out of Vraca, and he had a police belt with a holster, and then in the morgue in Visoko they managed to later on identify his body, his bones, using DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Apart from Adis's body, do you know of any additional bodies or remains that were discovered within the village of villagers who had been killed that UNPROFOR had not managed to discover?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And so apart from Adis's body, knowing about Adis's body being discovered sometime afterwards, you don't know about any other bodies being discovered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: My son Adis's body was the last to be discovered of all the people who died or who were killed in Stupni Do 28 days after he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the panel has been presented with evidence that UNPROFOR found, some days after the Stupni Do event, located 16 bodies. So there was a difference of some 22 bodies, Adis being one of them. Do you know anything about the other 21 bodies being found after UNPROFOR had left?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Among the bodies that were retrieved by UNPROFOR from my house, my son Adis was not among them, because I went twice to the morgue in Visoko and he was not there. His bones were not there. But only 20 days after he was killed, when the BH army entered Vares and liberated Vares, this is when Stupni Do was liberated too, and this is when his bones were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to the last exhibit in the booklet that you have in front of you. It's number 8461, and it's actually the last page because that's the B/C/S version which I want you to look at. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This is a list of deceased people who were killed in Stupni Do prepared and presented to a commission by Mr. Husnija Mahmutovic, and he lists some 38 villagers. I think you looked at this yesterday when we met. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think I asked you if you could -- you could identify from the list which of those persons were members of the ABiH who had been fighting in Stupni Do on that particular day. And did you inform me that Salko Likic, number 8, had been an ABiH member on at that day?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the same with number 10, Muharem Likic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: That's his son. Muhamed Likic. He was Salko Likic's son, but there is a mistake here. H. There was no H. Muamer, not Muhamer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Number 10 was also an ABiH member. Is it correct that you also mentioned number 11 and number 12? Rifet Likic and Samir Rahic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you also mentioned number 17, Zejnil Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And lastly, you mentioned number 30, Sefko Likic.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So apart from those six people, were all the other people on the list civilians who were killed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Likic Sulejman Medina was also a member of the BH army. Zejnil Mahmutovic -- or, rather, Edin Mahmutovic, Zejnil's son. Adis Likic, son of Kemal, my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was Adis involved in the defence of the village on that day?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was on the night-shift. Because he was not 18 yet he was a courier. He brought food.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And looking at this list of 38 people that you looked at yesterday, did you know each one of these people?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I think the witness did not complete with listing all the names from this list. I think that the Prosecutor interrupted him before he was finished. If I am mistaken, then I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I thought he had, but we'll go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The names which you mentioned which were serving ABiH members, again, Mr. Likic, were number 8, number 10, number 11, number 12 --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Twelve, 15, 16, 17, 27, and 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think you also mentioned 30.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I do apologise. Sefko Likic, son of Vejsil, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, is your son number 27?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is he on this list as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: On the day in question did you have any knowledge that he picked up a rifle and was fighting prior to being killed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: He was in my house. He did not have a rifle because not all of us had rifles. We didn't have enough weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What -- what was the arrangement with the weapons? You had -- you had two shifts. When one group of soldiers would relieve the other group of soldiers, would they bring weapons with them or would they take over the weapons which the operative soldiers were using?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. My colleague asked two leading questions and I did not intervene, but now he is on the border -- in fact, I think he crossed the border and I suggest that he should really take care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have exceeded the time allotted to you, so please conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What was the arrangements for the exchange of weapons? How did you share the weapons amongst your unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Again. Again. Now there's a suggestion that they shared the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It's obvious -- no. It's obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait. It is obvious for you. It may not be obvious for the Defence and not for the Judges. So please ask him without leading him in any way. Ask him had what was the situation regarding weapons. There were 42 men. How many weapons did they have, and how did they manage? And the Judges will draw the appropriate conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You've already told us how many weapons there were. You've already told us how many men there were in the unit. What was the arrangement in relation to the use of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: When the shifts rotated the weapons remained in positions with the exception of the seven rifles. We decided that four to five people should be on guard at any given time, and that's how it happened that day that there were five of them in Bogos. So that two or three weapons would always remain there. Naturally people took weapons home with them, and if a need arose a courier would come and would bring the weapons back to the line. And the rest of the weapons, up to 28, they would be there. Sometimes you would have 27 people in the trenches and only one piece would remain there, and sometimes there would be only two people in the trenches and so and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: My time is up. Just one last question. As regards the list of people prepared by Husnija Mahmutovic, did you know each one of these people?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Those are all my relatives and neighbours, because this was not a large village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And following the Stupni Do incident, have you ever seen any of these people again?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: No, never. I -- and it's impossible to see a dead man, dead person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. I apologise if I extended my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a very technical question to ask you. This village was defended by people on guard, 40 in total.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 42, interpreter's correction, in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You took part in the defence of that village, being in a trench. Here is my question: We were told that the HVO had taken control of the Bogos hill and then had entered the village. We would like to know whether the whole village was encircled and, if so, how you yourself were able to escape to the HVO. Tell me, after the fighting, when the HVO entered the village, what did you do yourself? Did you run away? Did you stay in the village? What happened?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: I went to my relative -- or, rather, my next door neighbour, Sacko Likic, and we headed towards the Bogos hill. We went up there and we couldn't proceed any further because the Bogos hill had been taken. The HVO soldiers had already started moving from the Bogos hill, and we encountered some other soldiers who survived there at the Bogos hill and maybe two or three other soldiers from our unit. So these were all the soldiers that were on the night-shift, and I myself was on the night-shift the night before, but they did not manage to pass through that route because we returned fire, the soldiers who had taken Bogos hill and that place in the plain. And so they bypassed, detoured this area, and they went to Prica Do, the hamlet. We remained where we were, and two women approached us, my wife, and I asked them, "Why did you come?" And they said, "We have come here --" I apologise. "We were sent here to tell you to surrender," and we should come back as soon as possible, and if we do so they will no longer kill people and burn the villages. But I made the decision, and everybody else who was there, we all decided that we would not be going back, because we had seen everything that had happened in the village. I personally saw that with my own eyes. So these two women and another soldier who was together with me, we managed to get to the free territory. UNPROFOR helped us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In light of what you've just said, the HVO may not have entirely surrounded the hill and the village as you remained on the hill, when your wife and the other woman came to ask you to surrender; is that right? And you stayed there, and after that you left.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from a purely technical and military --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Night fell, we went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and military standpoint. So you can confirm to me that the village was not entirely surrounded by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: The village -- well, partially -- I don't know how to express myself. It was not surrounded on all sides. There was a free area from the -- from the Strijezovo side. Forces of the Croatian Defence Council entered the village from the direction of Vares Majdan and Bijelo Borje, and afterwards the forces who took control of Bogos hill entered the village from the hamlet of Prica Do by my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to the way you are describing this, the HVO forces, well, some take control of the Bogos hill. Other men enter the village and come from Vares Majdan and Bijelo Borje.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to your estimation, how many were there? Give us a figure, an approximate figure, please. Were they greater in number than you were? Were there -- there more men or less?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure, but there were twice as many as there were us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying at least twice as much. There might have even been more than that.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, if not more. More, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how were they armed? Were they better equipped? Were they equipped like you, not so well-equipped?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: They were very well-armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: Do you know that members of the village guards during the fighting killed a number of HVO members? Do you know? Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Where I was they didn't, but about other places I can't say. I can't testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: This village was defended, and you have confirmed this, by guards. A witness came to tell us that a short while before that that people had come to the village to ask the villagers to hand over their weapons and to surrender. According to you, this is true, that a few days or a few weeks prior to that people came from Vares and asked you to surrender and to hand over your weapons?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat that question, please? Before the attack on Stupni Do. How long before the attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Attack, yes. A few days, a few weeks before. Before, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you not surrender? What could you do with just a few rifles in the face of units that were perhaps -- please answer the question. Why didn't you surrender?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not surrender in order to preserve the population. They wanted us to lay down our arms, to hand over our weapons, not just us to surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you hand over your weapons.?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL LIKIC
